    require_sqlite_foreign_keys_off ¶

    require_sqlite_foreign_keys_off(connection: Connection) -> None

    Refuse to migrate SQLite on a connection that enforces foreign keys.

    Alembic's batch mode is how a SQLite migration alters a table: it creates a copy with the new shape, copies the rows, drops the original and renames the copy. With PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON that DROP TABLE performs the foreign-key actions of the dropped table. Measured with Alembic 1.19.1 and SQLite 3.47.1: batch_alter_table("org", recreate="always") adding one nullable column to a parent whose children reference it with ON DELETE CASCADE took the child table from 3 rows to 0, and no statement raised.

    The engines the generated env.py and :class:AlembicHelper build never turn enforcement on, so only a connection the caller hands over as config.attributes["connection"] can carry it — typically one taken from an :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.AsyncDatabaseManager, which enforces foreign keys by default. The generated env.py calls this before running migrations on such a connection.

    Reads the pragma through the raw driver cursor, so the check neither opens a transaction nor changes how Alembic sees the connection. Any backend other than SQLite returns immediately.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    connection Connection

    The connection migrations are about to run on.

    		 required

    Raises:

    Type Description
    RuntimeError

    When connection is SQLite and PRAGMA foreign_keys answers 1.

    run_alembic_env ¶

    run_alembic_env(
    target_metadata: MetaData | Sequence[MetaData] | None,
    *,
    process_revision_directives: ProcessRevisionDirectives | None = None,
) -> None

    Run the current Alembic command the way the SDK configures it.

    Call it as the last statement of alembic/env.py. It resolves the database URL, applies alembic.ini's logging sections only when they exist, and runs the migrations offline (--sql) or online with compare_type, compare_server_default, batch mode, :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enum_migrations.render_enum_types as render_item, the enum-CHECK filter as include_object (so alembic check does not report drift on a clean SQLite schema) and the revision hooks.

    The URL comes from, in order: the sqlalchemy.url already on the config (--database-url, or AlembicHelper(db_url=...)); the DATABASE_URL environment variable; a settings object on core/settings.py under either code root (src or app) — a BaseSettings instance or a zero-arg factory such as get_settings(); and finally DATABASE_URL in the project's .env. alembic.ini never has to hold a secret.

    Online, three entry points are checked in order:

    1. A caller that already holds a connection hands it over as config.attributes["connection"] (Alembic's connection-sharing recipe, typically from inside AsyncConnection.run_sync), and the migrations run on it: no engine and no event loop of our own. A SQLite connection that enforces foreign keys is refused first (:func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.migrations.require_sqlite_foreign_keys_off): batch mode recreates tables, and dropping a parent's old copy cascades to its children.
    2. No event loop is running in this thread (the CLI, the sync AlembicHelper methods, or its *_async methods, which run in a worker thread): build an async engine under asyncio.run.
    3. An event loop is running and no connection was handed over: raise before creating the coroutine, because asyncio.run cannot nest and would leave the migration coroutine un-awaited.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    target_metadata MetaData | Sequence[MetaData] | None

    The autogenerate target, usually BaseModel.metadata. None disables autogenerate comparisons.

    		 required
    process_revision_directives ProcessRevisionDirectives | None

    The hook every autogenerated revision goes through. None composes :data:DEFAULT_REVISION_HOOKS.

    		 None

    Raises:

    Type Description
    RuntimeError

    When no source provides a database URL — the message is :data:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.migrations.MISSING_DATABASE_URL_MESSAGE, the same one the AlembicHelper reads raise, followed by the cause of every attempt that failed, so an import error inside core/settings.py reaches the operator instead of a bare "DATABASE_URL is empty"; in case 3; and in case 1 when the connection is SQLite with PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON.

    DEFAULT_REVISION_HOOKS module-attribute ¶

    DEFAULT_REVISION_HOOKS: Final[tuple[ProcessRevisionDirectives, ...]] = (
    reorder_base_columns_first,
    backfill_non_nullable_defaults,
    sync_enum_types,
    sqlite_enum_checks,
    create_enum_types_on_add_column,
    drop_enum_types_on_downgrade,
)

    The process_revision_directives hooks every revision goes through.

    In order:

    • reorder_base_columns_first: id, is_active, created_at and updated_at come first in every create_table.
    • backfill_non_nullable_defaults: a NOT NULL column added to a table with rows gets a server_default from its scalar Python default, so the migration backfills existing rows instead of raising NotNullViolationError.
    • sync_enum_types: a changed enum member list becomes a replace_enum operation. Alembic compares neither pg_enum (PostgreSQL) nor the CHECK constraint (SQLite), so without it, adding a member to a Python enum autogenerates an empty migration.
    • sqlite_enum_checks: every enum add_column gets its own, per-column CHECK on SQLite (two columns of one enum used to share a name, and the batch kept one), and every enum drop_column drops its CHECK first (the batch rebuilt the table with a check naming the dropped column). No-op on PostgreSQL.
    • create_enum_types_on_add_column: an enum column added to an existing table creates its PostgreSQL ENUM first — add_column never does, and the ALTER TABLE failed with type ... does not exist.
    • drop_enum_types_on_downgrade: the downgrade of a new table also drops the PostgreSQL ENUM types no surviving table uses, so a downgrade followed by an upgrade does not fail with type ... already exists.

    Extend it with compose_hooks(*DEFAULT_REVISION_HOOKS, my_hook) and pass the result as process_revision_directives=.

    enable_sqlite_foreign_keys ¶

    enable_sqlite_foreign_keys(engine: AsyncEngine) -> None

    Make SQLite enforce FOREIGN KEY constraints on every connection.

    SQLite parses REFERENCES clauses but only checks them on a connection that ran PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON — off is the compiled-in default, and the setting lives on the connection, not on the database file. Left off, three things pass on SQLite that PostgreSQL rejects or does differently. Measured on SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 and 2.1.3 with aiosqlite 0.22.1, SQLite 3.47.1:

    ======================================== =========== ============== Operation FK off FK on ======================================== =========== ============== insert a child pointing at no parent accepted IntegrityError delete a parent, ON DELETE CASCADE child stays child deleted add_all([child, parent]) with no accepted IntegrityError relationship() ordering the flush ======================================== =========== ==============

    The pragma is emitted from a connect listener on engine.sync_engine, through the raw driver cursor, so it runs once per new connection and before any transaction opens. SQLite ignores PRAGMA foreign_keys inside a transaction: emitted after :func:enable_sqlite_savepoints has issued BEGIN it is a silent no-op and the pragma keeps answering 0.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    engine AsyncEngine

    The SQLite engine to configure. Emitting this pragma against another backend would fail, so callers building their own engine must gate on the backend.

    		 required
    Notes

    Do not run Alembic batch migrations on a connection with this on. Batch mode rebuilds a table by creating a copy and dropping the original, and with enforcement on the DROP TABLE runs the foreign-key actions: measured with Alembic 1.19.1, batch_alter_table("org", recreate="always") on a parent with ON DELETE CASCADE children deleted every child row without raising. :func:require_sqlite_foreign_keys_off is the check the generated env.py runs before migrating.

    enable_sqlite_savepoints ¶

    enable_sqlite_savepoints(engine: AsyncEngine) -> None

    Make SAVEPOINT behave on SQLite the way it does on PostgreSQL.

    The pysqlite driver that aiosqlite builds on opens transactions implicitly and, by default, never emits a BEGIN. SQLite therefore sees the SAVEPOINT as the outermost transaction, and the matching RELEASE SAVEPOINT commits it. The damage is invisible on the failure path — a rollback to the savepoint still works — and only shows up when a nested block exits cleanly and the surrounding transaction is later rolled back: the supposedly pending rows are already durable.

    That is the difference between the SDK's production backend and its test backend silently disagreeing about atomicity, so the manager applies SQLAlchemy's documented remedy to every SQLite engine it builds: turn off the driver's implicit transaction handling, then emit BEGIN explicitly when SQLAlchemy starts a transaction.

    Idempotent per engine — re-registering the same handlers is harmless, and the listeners are attached to engine.sync_engine because the driver-level events fire there, not on the async facade.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    engine AsyncEngine

    The SQLite engine to configure. Passing a non-SQLite engine would break its transaction handling, so callers building their own engine must gate on the backend.

    		 required

    A third listener closes the hole a failed COMMIT leaves behind. When SQLite refuses the COMMIT (database is locked), the transaction stays open on the driver connection, but SQLAlchemy has already marked its own transaction inactive: closing the :class:~sqlalchemy.engine.Connection neither rolls back nor lets the pool do it (the pool is told the transaction was reset). The connection goes back to the pool inside the open transaction, and its next user fails on BEGIN with cannot start a transaction within a transaction. The reset listener rolls back on check-in whenever the driver still reports in_transaction.

    Measured with aiosqlite 0.22.1 and SQLite 3.47.1 in the rollback journal. A COMMIT forced to fail (another connection holding a read transaction, busy_timeout of 0.1 s) left the connection dirty every time on SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 and 2.1.3 without this listener, and clean with it. Two read-modify-write transactions racing on one file, on 2.0.52, had the first COMMIT refused in 8 to 11 of 200 trials per run, with busy_timeout unset, 0.1 s or 30 s alike, and every refusal left a dirty connection; with the listener, 6 of 200 refused and none dirty. In WAL mode a reader does not block COMMIT, and the same race refused 0 of 200.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    engine AsyncEngine

    The SQLite engine to configure. Passing a non-SQLite engine would break its transaction handling, so callers building their own engine must gate on the backend.

    		 required
    Notes

    tests/db/test_transaction.py pins the RELEASE path, which is the one that regressed silently before this existed. tests/db/test_sqlite_failed_commit.py pins the failed COMMIT path.

    enable_sqlite_wal ¶

    enable_sqlite_wal(engine: AsyncEngine) -> None

    Put every connection of a SQLite engine in WAL mode.

    In the default rollback journal a reader and a writer exclude each other, so the moment an application grows a worker — web process and taskiq worker on one app.db — the second one fails. Measured across two processes, one holding a read transaction open while the other inserts:

    ================== ========================================== journal_mode Result for the writer ================== ========================================== delete waits the whole busy_timeout, then sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked wal commits immediately ================== ==========================================

    WAL is a property of the database file, not of the connection: setting it once is enough, it survives the process, and every later connection from any process opens the file already in WAL. Emitting the pragma per connection is therefore idempotent, and it is done per connection only so the very first connection of a brand-new file switches it too. On an in-memory database the pragma is a no-op — SQLite answers memory and keeps its own journal, without error.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    engine AsyncEngine

    The SQLite engine to configure. Emitting this pragma against another backend would fail, so callers building their own engine must gate on the backend.

    		 required
    Notes

    WAL admits one writer at a time; the others queue (see sqlite_busy_timeout). What no amount of waiting fixes is a transaction that reads first and writes later — promoting the lock fails at once when another connection wrote in between, and busy_timeout does not apply because there is nothing to wait for. Claim the row, do the long work with no session open, then persist.

    transaction async ¶

    transaction(session: AsyncSession) -> AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]

    Group every write on session into a single commit.

    While the block is open, repository writes flush instead of committing, so nothing is durable until the outermost block exits cleanly. An exception rolls the whole block back and propagates.

    Nesting is re-entrant — an inner block joins the outer one and does not commit on its own exit. The depth is restored before the commit or rollback runs, so the repository is already back to its normal mode by the time that statement is issued.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    session AsyncSession

    The session to bind the block to. Every repository sharing this session joins the same block.

    		 required

    Yields:

    Name Type Description
    AsyncSession AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]

    The same session, so ``async with transaction(s) as
    session AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]

    `` reads naturally at the call site.

    Raises:

    Type Description
    BaseException

    Re-raises whatever the body raised, after rolling back at the outermost level.
    Notes

    Catching an exception inside the block and continuing leaves the session in a failed state — SQLAlchemy requires a rollback after a failed flush. Wrap the fallible part in :func:savepoint when you intend to recover from it.

    savepoint async ¶

    savepoint(session: AsyncSession) -> AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]

    Run a nested, individually revertible unit of work.

    Issues a real SAVEPOINT via session.begin_nested(). A failure inside the block rolls back to the savepoint and leaves the surrounding transaction usable, which is what lets a caller catch a :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.exceptions.conflict.ConflictException and carry on:

    async with transaction(session):
    await accounts.add(account)
    try:
        async with savepoint(session):
            await nicknames.add(nickname)
    except ConflictException:
        pass  # the account survives, the nickname is rolled back

    The block behaves like :func:transaction for repository writes — it bumps the same depth counter, so writes inside it flush rather than commit and the outer block still owns the final commit.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    session AsyncSession

    The session to open the savepoint on.

    		 required

    Yields:

    Name Type Description
    AsyncSession AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]

    The same session.

    Raises:

    Type Description
    BaseException

    Re-raises whatever the body raised, after rolling back to the savepoint.
    Notes

    PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT unconditionally. SQLite needs :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.connection.enable_sqlite_savepoints, which :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.connection.AsyncDatabaseManager applies to every SQLite engine it builds — without it the driver's implicit transaction handling turns the closing RELEASE SAVEPOINT into a commit, so a nested block that exits cleanly becomes durable even when the outer block is later rolled back. A session built from a hand-rolled SQLite engine must call that function itself.

    The configuration decides which stemmer and stop-word list apply, so it is what makes comprou match comprar in Portuguese and buying match buy in English. :attr:SIMPLE disables both — it lowercases and splits on non-word characters, nothing more, which is the right choice for identifiers, SKUs and tags.

    Members cover the Snowball configurations shipped by every supported PostgreSQL release. A database with a custom configuration created through CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION is out of scope; the value reaches PostgreSQL as a regconfig, which rejects an unknown name with a clear error rather than silently matching nothing.

    Ignored entirely on backends without full-text support, where the query degrades to the ILIKE layer.

    TextSearchWeightEnum ¶

    Bases: BaseStrEnum

    Relative importance of a column in the relevance score.

    PostgreSQL ranks A highest and D lowest, so a term found in a title outranks the same term buried in a body. Only meaningful for :func:full_text_condition and :func:full_text_rank; the ILIKE layer has no score to weight.

    TempestEnum ¶

    TempestEnum(*enums: Any, **kwargs: Any)

    Bases: Enum

    A SQLAlchemy Enum configured to be safe on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

    Differs from sqlalchemy.Enum in exactly the three defaults described in the module docstring: the column stores member values, a CHECK constraint is emitted on backends without a native enum type, and the generated PostgreSQL type name carries a suffix.

    Every default can still be overridden per column — passing name="legacy_status" keeps an existing type, and create_constraint=False opts a column out of the SQLite check (useful only when migrating a table that already holds invalid data you have not cleaned yet).

    The resulting DDL:

    -- PostgreSQL
CREATE TYPE order_status_enum AS ENUM ('open', 'in_progress');
status order_status_enum NOT NULL

-- SQLite
status VARCHAR(11) NOT NULL
CONSTRAINT ck_order_status CHECK (status IN ('open', 'in_progress'))

    The CHECK name follows :data:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.model.NAMING_CONVENTION, so it is stable across machines and Alembic can address it by name.

    Notes

    That name is derived from the enum type, not the column, so two columns of the same enum in one table would produce two CHECK constraints sharing a name. SQLite accepts that in CREATE TABLE, but Alembic's batch mode keys constraints by name and keeps only one, so the other column silently accepted any value after the next rebuild (#526). The second and later columns of one enum in a table therefore get ck_<table>_<enum>_<column>; the first keeps ck_<table>_<enum>, as does every table with one column per enum, so no constraint already applied changes name. NAMING_CONVENTION itself is untouched.

    The same holds for a migration written by alembic revision --autogenerate through the SDK's env.py: :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enum_migrations.render_enum_types omits the CHECK the type attaches, and the sa.Enum(..., create_constraint=True) rendered on the column recreates it where it belongs. Without that, SQLAlchemy 2.1 with Alembic 1.20.0 rendered two explicit CheckConstraint per enum column, both named ck_<table>_<enum> by the convention, and PostgreSQL refused the second one.

    Configure the enum type before handing off to SQLAlchemy.

    Only fills in defaults the caller left out, so an explicit keyword always wins.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    *enums Any

    Either a single enum.Enum subclass or a sequence of string values, exactly as sqlalchemy.Enum accepts.

    		 ()
    **kwargs Any

    Forwarded to sqlalchemy.Enum. name, native_enum, create_constraint and values_callable are defaulted when absent.

    		 {}

    Return the deterministic database type name for enum_class.

    Deterministic because the name has to match across three places that never see each other: the model's DDL, the migration that creates the type, and the migration that later replaces it. OrderStatus becomes order_status_enum, and so does OrderStatusEnum: one trailing :data:ENUM_CLASS_SUFFIX is dropped before the suffix is appended, so the class suffix and the type suffix never stack into order_status_enum_enum. A class called exactly Enum keeps its name.

    Notes

    Until the suffix was dropped, a class ending in Enum produced the doubled name. A database created then still holds it, and PostgreSQL refuses every statement that casts to the new name (type "order_status_enum" does not exist) until the type is renamed. :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enum_migrations.sync_enum_types detects the rename on autogenerate and emits :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enum_migrations.RenameEnumTypeOp; a column that has to keep the old name passes it explicitly, mapped_column(TempestEnum(OrderStatusEnum, name="order_status_enum_enum")).

    Bases: MigrateOperation

    Rename an enum type, keeping its members and every column's data.

    alembic revision --autogenerate never notices a renamed type: on PostgreSQL the columns keep pointing at the old pg_type row and the model points at a name that does not exist, so every statement that casts to it fails with type "<new>" does not exist. :func:sync_enum_types detects the rename and emits this operation; it is also callable by hand as op.rename_enum_type("candidate_slug_enum_enum", "candidate_slug_enum", columns=[...]).

    • PostgreSQL: ALTER TYPE <old> RENAME TO <new>. The columns follow the type, so columns is not needed there.
    • SQLite: there is no type; the name lives in each column's CHECK (ck_<table>_<old>). Every listed column's table is rebuilt with the check renamed, so the name matches what the model declares and alembic check stops reporting it.

    Reversible: :meth:reverse swaps the two names.

    render_enum_types ¶

    render_enum_types(
    type_: str, obj: object, autogen_context: AutogenContext
) -> str | Literal[False]

    Render an SDK column type as a self-contained SQLAlchemy type.

    Alembic's default renders a type it does not know as a dotted path into this package — tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.… — which the generated migration never imports, so the file raises NameError (or F821 under lint) the first time it runs. Two SDK types hit that path:

    • :class:TempestEnum renders as sa.Enum with the members spelled out, which avoids the import and freezes the members as they were when the migration was written — what a migration is supposed to record.
    • :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.UtcDateTime renders as sa.TIMESTAMP(timezone=True), the exact DDL it emits. The Python-side normalization it adds is a runtime behaviour of the model, not of the schema, so a migration has no reason to carry it.

    It also omits the CHECK constraint that an Enum (or a Boolean) column carries because of its type — the one SQLAlchemy marks _type_bound. The sa.Enum(..., create_constraint=True) rendered on the column already recreates that CHECK where the backend needs it (SQLite), and PostgreSQL uses the native type. Alembic means to skip it on its own, but recognizes it only through constraint._create_rule.target, which SQLAlchemy 2.1 no longer sets; there the migration came out with two explicit CheckConstraint per enum column, and PostgreSQL refused the second (check constraint "ck_<table>_<enum>" already exists). A CheckConstraint declared in __table_args__ is not type bound and keeps rendering.

    Wire it into env.py as render_item=render_enum_types.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    type_ str

    What Alembic is rendering ("type", "check", "column", …).

    		 required
    obj object

    The object to render.

    		 required
    autogen_context AutogenContext

    Alembic's rendering context.

    		 required

    Returns:

    Type Description
    str | Literal[False]

    str | Literal[False]: The rendered expression; None (typed as
    str | Literal[False]

    Literal[False], see _OMIT_FROM_MIGRATION) to omit the
    str | Literal[False]

    object from the migration; or False to let Alembic render it
    str | Literal[False]

    its own way. The annotation is Alembic's RenderItemFn, so the

    sync_enum_types ¶

    sync_enum_types(
    context: MigrationContext,
    revision: str | Iterable[str | None],
    directives: list[MigrationScript],
) -> None

    Append :class:ReplaceEnumOp for every enum whose members changed.

    An alembic revision --autogenerate hook. Reads the enum members the database currently enforces, compares them with the metadata, and emits a replacement for each difference — the gap that makes adding a member to a Python enum a silent no-op today.

    Detection is best-effort by design: an enum the backend cannot report on is skipped rather than diffed against a guess, because emitting a wrong replace_enum would drop values from live rows. PostgreSQL is read from pg_enum; SQLite from the generated CHECK constraint, and only when it still has the generated shape.

    A renamed type is detected too, and emitted as :class:RenameEnumTypeOp ahead of any replacement — the case :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enums.enum_type_name creates for a class ending in Enum, whose type used to be <name>_enum_enum. On PostgreSQL the declared type is missing and every column it types is still typed by one other existing enum that the metadata no longer declares; on SQLite the column's enum CHECK carries a name that differs from the declared one only where the enum name sits.

    Bases: MigrateOperation

    Create the CHECK that enforces an enum column on SQLite.

    SQLite has no enum type: the members live in a CHECK named by the naming convention. Left to sa.Enum(create_constraint=True) inside batch_alter_table, that check is named after the type, so two columns of one enum produce two checks under one name and the batch, which keys constraints by name, keeps only the last — the other column then accepts any value, with nothing reporting it. This operation names the check explicitly, per column.

    It is a no-op on every other backend: PostgreSQL enforces the members through the native type and carries no CHECK.

    :func:sqlite_enum_checks emits it after every enum add_column (and after a create_table whose columns share an enum); it is also callable by hand as op.create_enum_check(...) or, inside a batch, batch_op.create_enum_check(...).

    DropEnumCheckOp ¶

    DropEnumCheckOp(table_name: str, column_name: str, *, schema: str | None = None)

    Bases: MigrateOperation

    Drop the SQLite CHECK of an enum column, before dropping the column.

    SQLite's batch mode copies every reflected CHECK into the rebuilt table and cannot tell which column a check text names, so batch_op.drop_column("age_range") rebuilt the table with CHECK (age_range IN (...)) still attached and failed with no such column: age_range — the downgrade of every enum add_column broke. This operation reads the table's checks, picks the ones in the generated <column> IN (...) shape for this column, and drops them by name, whatever name they carry.

    It is a no-op on every other backend. :func:sqlite_enum_checks emits it before every enum drop_column.

    sqlite_enum_checks ¶

    sqlite_enum_checks(
    context: MigrationContext,
    revision: str | Iterable[str | None],
    directives: list[MigrationScript],

    Give every enum column its own SQLite CHECK, and drop it with the column.

    An alembic revision --autogenerate hook, for the two places where the CHECK an sa.Enum(create_constraint=True) carries goes wrong under the batch mode the SDK's env.py turns on:

    • Adding a column. The check is named after the enum type, so two columns of one enum get two checks under one name, and the batch keeps one. Every enum add_column is rewritten to create_constraint=False and followed by :class:CreateEnumCheckOp, named as the model's metadata names that column's check — ck_<table>_<enum>, or ck_<table>_<enum>_<column> for the second and later columns of one enum in a table (:class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enums.TempestEnum). A create_table whose columns share an enum gets the same treatment for those later columns.
    • Dropping a column. The batch copies the reflected check that names the column into the rebuilt table, which then fails with no such column. Every enum drop_column is preceded by :class:DropEnumCheckOp.

    Both operations are no-ops outside SQLite, so the same migration runs on PostgreSQL with no CHECK at all. Both the upgrade and the downgrade are rewritten. Compose it with the other hooks through :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.alembic_hooks.compose_hooks.

    CreateEnumTypeOp(name: str, values: Sequence[str], *, schema: str | None = None)

    Bases: MigrateOperation

    Create a PostgreSQL ENUM type, and do nothing on other backends.

    op.create_table creates the native type of its enum columns; op.add_column does not, so adding an enum column whose type is new to an existing table failed with type "<name>" does not exist. :func:create_enum_types_on_add_column puts this operation ahead of such an add_column; it is also callable by hand as op.create_enum_type("order_status_enum", ["open", "done"]).

    Online, the type is created only when it does not exist yet, so a type another table already uses is left alone. In offline (--sql) mode there is no connection to ask, and a plain CREATE TYPE is written. SQLite has no type — the members live in a CHECK — so the operation is a no-op there.

    Put :class:CreateEnumTypeOp ahead of an add_column with a new enum.

    An alembic revision --autogenerate hook. Only create_table creates the PostgreSQL ENUM its columns use; adding an enum column whose type is new to an existing table rendered just ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN age_source age_source_enum, which failed with type "age_source_enum" does not exist. For each native enum type an add_column uses, the hook inserts op.create_enum_type(name, values) before the operation (before the whole batch block, when there is one) — unless a create_table of the same revision creates it, or a column the revision does not touch already uses it. The upgrade and the downgrade are both handled: a downgrade that re-adds a dropped enum column recreates its type the same way.

    The operation checks pg_type before creating, so a type that exists is never recreated, and it is a no-op outside PostgreSQL.

    Bases: MigrateOperation

    Drop a PostgreSQL ENUM type, and do nothing on other backends.

    op.drop_table removes the table but not the native type its create_table created, so a downgrade followed by an upgrade fails with type "<name>" already exists. This operation emits DROP TYPE IF EXISTS, which is safe to run when the type is already gone. SQLite has no type to drop — the enum lives in a CHECK that leaves with its table — so the operation is a no-op there and on every other backend.

    :func:drop_enum_types_on_downgrade appends it to autogenerated downgrades; it is also callable by hand as op.drop_enum_type("order_status_enum").

    drop_enum_types_on_downgrade(
    context: MigrationContext,

    directives: list[MigrationScript],

    Append :class:DropEnumTypeOp after the tables and columns a downgrade drops.

    An alembic revision --autogenerate hook. The downgrade Alembic writes for a new table is only op.drop_table(...), and for a new column only drop_column(...); both leave the PostgreSQL ENUM type behind, so the next upgrade fails with type "<name>" already exists. For every native enum type used by a table or a column this downgrade drops, the hook appends op.drop_enum_type(name) at the end of the downgrade — but only when nothing that survives the downgrade still uses it: every column of the type in the metadata is dropped (with its table or on its own), and no table or column the downgrade recreates declares it. A type shared by two tables is therefore dropped by the revision that removes the last one.

    The decision is made from the metadata alone, with no database connection, and the operation itself is a no-op outside PostgreSQL, so the same migration runs on SQLite. Compose it with the other hooks through :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.alembic_hooks.compose_hooks.

    type_bound_check_include_object ¶

    type_bound_check_include_object(
    metadata: MetaData | Sequence[MetaData] | None,
) -> Callable[[object, str | None, str, bool, object], bool]

    Build the include_object filter that hides enum CHECK drift.

    Alembic's CHECK comparison reads the constraint from the database but drops it from the metadata side: it collects metadata CHECKs through all_table_check_constraints, which skips the ones a column's type attaches (SQLAlchemy marks them _type_bound). On SQLite — where an Enum column is a VARCHAR plus a CHECK — the database therefore always shows one constraint the metadata does not, and alembic check fails on a clean upgrade head proposing remove_constraint for ck_<table>_<enum>.

    A reflected CHECK whose name matches a type-bound CHECK declared in metadata on the same table is not drift: the column type recreates it. Returning False skips it; every other object is left to Alembic. The table is part of the key because two tables may carry a check of the same name under a project's own naming convention, and a match on the name alone would hide one table's drift behind the other's.

    A reflected enum-shaped CHECK (<column> IN (...)) on a column the metadata types with a check-carrying enum is hidden too, whatever its name. Its name can legitimately differ from the declared one — after :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.enums.enum_type_name stopped doubling the _enum suffix, or in a table an older SDK rebuilt — and the name-only match then proposed remove_constraint for the check that enforces the column. Renames and member changes are :func:sync_enum_types' job, which reads the same check.

    Pass it as include_object in context.configure; :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.alembic_env.run_alembic_env does.

    Name Type Description Default
    metadata MetaData | Sequence[MetaData] | None

    reorder_base_columns_first ¶

    reorder_base_columns_first(
    context: MigrationContext,
    revision: str | Iterable[str | None],
    directives: list[MigrationScript],
) -> None

    Reorder columns inside every autogenerated CreateTableOp.

    SQLAlchemy stores columns in declaration order, which already matches what BaseModel defines (id → updated_at). Autogenerate normally honors that, but third-party mixins or class composition can flip the order in ways that leak into the migration. This hook normalizes it:

    • The four BaseModel columns (id, is_active, created_at, updated_at) come first, in that exact order.
    • Constraints stay where Alembic placed them (typically right after the columns they reference).
    • Every other column keeps its original relative position.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    context MigrationContext

    The active Alembic context.

    		 required
    revision str | Iterable[str | None]

    The new revision identifier — unused.

    		 required
    directives list[MigrationScript]

    The list of MigrationScript directives Alembic will render. Modified in-place.

    		 required
    Notes

    Nested directives (ModifyTableOps and friends) are recursed into, so the reorder applies inside a batch operation too.

    backfill_non_nullable_defaults ¶

    backfill_non_nullable_defaults(
    context: MigrationContext,
    revision: str | Iterable[str | None],
    directives: list[MigrationScript],
) -> None

    Give every added NOT NULL column a backfilling server_default.

    Adding a NOT NULL column to a table that already has rows explodes on PostgreSQL with NotNullViolationError: column "x" contains null values — because a Python-side default= only fires on ORM inserts, never as DDL. Autogenerate therefore emits op.add_column(sa.Column("x", ..., nullable=False)) with no server_default, and the database has no value to backfill the existing rows with.

    This hook closes that gap: for every autogenerated AddColumnOp whose column is nullable=False, carries no server_default already, and does declare a scalar Python default= (the value you intended new rows to get), it copies that default into a server_default so the generated migration backfills existing rows in the same statement. The column keeps the value as its DB default afterwards — harmless and matching the model's intent.

    What it deliberately does not touch:

    • CreateTableOp columns — a brand-new table has no rows, so a bare NOT NULL is already safe.
    • Columns with a callable / SQL-expression default (uuid4, func.now()) or no default at all — those cannot be backfilled deterministically and need a hand-written data migration.
    • Columns that already carry a server_default.

    Compose it after :func:reorder_base_columns_first::

    process_revision_directives=compose_hooks(
    reorder_base_columns_first,
    backfill_non_nullable_defaults,
)

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    context MigrationContext

    The active Alembic context — unused.

    		 required
    revision str | Iterable[str | None]

    The new revision identifier — unused.

    		 required
    directives list[MigrationScript]

    The MigrationScript directives Alembic will render. Mutated in-place.

    		 required

    ENUM_CLASS_SUFFIX module-attribute ¶

    ENUM_CLASS_SUFFIX: Final[str] = 'Enum'

    Class-name suffix :func:enum_type_name drops before naming the type.

    A project that names its enums CandidateSlugEnum would otherwise get candidate_slug_enum_enum: the class suffix and :data:ENUM_TYPE_SUFFIX say the same thing twice. Dropping one trailing Enum makes CandidateSlugEnum and CandidateSlug produce the same type name, so adopting or dropping the suffix in a later refactor no longer renames the database type.

    ENUM_TYPE_SUFFIX module-attribute ¶

    ENUM_TYPE_SUFFIX: Final[str] = '_enum'

    Suffix appended to a generated PostgreSQL ENUM type name.

    PostgreSQL keeps types and tables in the same namespace, so a type named after the enum class alone (status) collides with a table or column called status. The suffix makes OrderStatus become order_status_enum, which is unambiguous and still readable in \dT output and in a migration diff.

    WhereClause module-attribute ¶

    WhereClause = Q | ColumnElement[bool]

    What a repository's where= accepts.

    Either a :class:Q tree, which resolves lazily against the repository's model, or a SQLAlchemy clause that is already bound to its columns. The second form is what lets a condition built elsewhere — a text search, a hand-written and_ — flow into list / paginate / cursor_paginate without being re-expressed as filter keywords.

    NAMING_CONVENTION module-attribute ¶

    NAMING_CONVENTION: dict[str, str] = {
    "ix": "ix_%(column_0_N_label)s",
    "uq": "uq_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_N_name)s",
    "ck": "ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s",
    "fk": "fk_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_N_name)s_%(referred_table_name)s",
    "pk": "pk_%(table_name)s",
}

    Alembic-friendly naming convention applied to every constraint.

    Constraint names become deterministic across machines and DB engines, so alembic revision --autogenerate only emits real schema diffs instead of churn from auto-generated identifiers.

    Composite unique constraints, indexes and foreign keys are named after every column, joined with _: UniqueConstraint("title", "release_year") on books is uq_books_title_release_year. The column_0_N_* tokens SQLAlchemy expands render a one-column constraint exactly like the column_0_* tokens did, so a single-column name (uq_books_title, ix_books_title) is the same as before by construction.

    Until the composite fix the templates read only the first column (:data:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.naming.LEGACY_NAMING_CONVENTION), so UniqueConstraint("title") and UniqueConstraint("title", "release_year") were both uq_books_title: PostgreSQL refuses the second with relation "uq_books_title" already exists while SQLite accepts both. A database created under that convention holds the old names for its composite constraints; :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.naming.legacy_constraint_renames lists them and writes the RENAME statements.

    A name longer than the dialect's identifier limit (63 characters on PostgreSQL) is shortened by SQLAlchemy when it emits the DDL: the first 55 characters, _, and the last four hex digits of the full name's MD5 — the same on every run. SQLite has no limit and keeps the full name. Joining with _ leaves one ambiguity the convention cannot remove: columns ("a_b", "c") and ("a", "b_c") render the same name, and such a pair needs an explicit name=.

    ColumnRef module-attribute ¶

    ColumnRef = str | InstrumentedAttribute[Any]

    A searchable column: its name, or the mapped attribute itself.

    BaseUserRefreshTokenModel ¶

    Bases: BaseModel

    Abstract opaque-refresh-token row used by the bundled auth flow.

    Concrete subclasses pick the __tablename__ (user_refresh_tokens by convention) and add the FK to the project's concrete UserModel. The SDK never sees the plaintext after the issuance response — only the hash is persisted.

    Attributes:

    Name Type Description
    user_id UUID

    Owner of the token. Concrete subclasses MUST declare this as a ForeignKey so cascading deletes wipe the tokens alongside the user.
    token_hash str

    SHA-256 hex digest of the plaintext refresh token. Indexed + unique so lookups by hash are fast and duplicates impossible.
    family_id UUID

    Rotation lineage. Every token minted by rotating an existing one inherits its family_id; a brand-new login starts a fresh family. Reuse detection and logout operate on the whole family at once.
    expires_at datetime

    UTC timestamp the token becomes invalid. Defaults to JWT_REFRESH_TTL_SECONDS after issuance.
    used_at datetime | None

    UTC timestamp the token was rotated (consumed by a successful refresh). Non-null means the token is spent — replaying it triggers reuse detection.
    revoked_at datetime | None

    UTC timestamp the token was explicitly revoked (logout or family-wide reuse kill). Non-null means the token is dead regardless of its expiry.
    amr str | None

    Space-separated RFC 8176 methods the family was authenticated with ("pwd", "pwd otp", "ext", "hwk"), copied onto every token minted by rotating it, so a refresh never promotes a session to MFA. NULL on a row written before the column existed: the access tokens it mints carry no amr and count as "no second factor".

    UserTokenPurposeEnum ¶

    Bases: StrEnum

    What a token authorizes when redeemed.

    Each value maps to a distinct flow exposed by :class:tempest_fastapi_sdk.auth.UserAuthService:

    • ACTIVATION — confirm the email address the user signed up with.
    • PASSWORD_RESET — let the user pick a new password without the old one.
    • EMAIL_VERIFICATION — re-verify the user's current email (resend the confirmation link).
    • EMAIL_CHANGE — confirm a move to a new email address. The pending new address travels in the token row's :attr:BaseUserTokenModel.payload.

    BaseVoiceProfileModel ¶

    Bases: BaseModel

    Abstract enrolled voiceprint belonging to one user.

    Concrete subclasses pick the __tablename__ (user_voice_profiles by convention) and add the FK to the project's concrete UserModel.

    Attributes:

    Name Type Description
    user_id UUID

    Owner of the voiceprint. Concrete subclasses MUST declare this as a ForeignKey so a cascading delete takes the biometric data with the account.
    label str | None

    What this recording was — "cadastro no onboarding", "ligação de 12/08". A person may hold several profiles, and knowing which is which is what makes it possible to delete the bad one.
    embedding bytes

    The voiceprint, float32 little-endian. Stored as bytes rather than an array column so the table works on SQLite and Postgres alike; dimensions says how many values it holds.
    dimensions int

    Length of the vector. Checked on read — a profile written by a different model must not be silently compared against one from the current model, because the similarity would be a number without meaning.
    model_name str

    Which embedding model produced it. Swapping models invalidates every profile, and this column is how you find the ones that need re-enrolling.
    consent_at datetime

    When the person consented to voice biometrics. Required — the service refuses to write a row without it.
    consent_reference str

    What they consented to: a policy version, a signed document id, a ticket. Free text because what counts as evidence differs per product, but not nullable, because "we have consent" with nothing behind it is not a record.
    last_matched_at datetime | None

    Last time this profile matched a voice. NULL until it does.
